title: Solidarity
hookLine: stub a toe and the whole body stops: Paul's picture, stretched to the whole human race

lines: A STUBBED TOE STOPS THE BODY.
cards: Stub a toe on the bed frame at night, and the whole body stops. Hands reach down. The face winces.
A word comes out that wouldn't be said in church. Nobody called a meeting. Paul uses that picture, writing to the Christians at Corinth about how they belong to each other.
In the Douay-Rheims: "if one member suffer any thing, all the members suffer with it; or if one member glory, all the members rejoice with it."
Catholic social teaching stretches that one body past the church door, to the whole human race. Today, solidarity.

teach.b: In Acts, Paul stands before the council in Athens, among people whose gods are not his, and tells them, in the Douay-Rheims, that God "hath made of one, all mankind, to dwell upon the whole face of the earth."
Made of one. Catholic teaching reads that as one human family, whatever the borders, languages or religions. Second, what solidarity is not.
John Paul the Second wrote that it isn't a feeling of vague pity at the troubles of people far away.

It's a firm, lasting commitment to the common good, to the good of all and of each, because everyone is responsible for everyone. A feeling passes when the news changes. A commitment keeps showing up.
Third, how close the far-off already is. The shirt on your back was sewn somewhere; the coffee was picked by someone. Lives on opposite sides of the earth are already tied together.
Solidarity asks that those ties be just, that the person at the other end of the thread is treated as family.
Paul gives the daily version to the Galatians: "Bear ye one another's burdens."
Fourth, it runs both ways. Look again at Paul's line. When one member suffers, all suffer; when one member is honored, all rejoice.
Solidarity isn't only pity flowing downhill. It's also learning from, celebrating with, and receiving from people far away. One family shares the grief and the feast.

how: Catholics pray for people around the world in the prayers of the faithful at Mass, and some parishes support relief and development work abroad, sometimes through partnerships with a parish in another country.

games.q: you're Paul, standing before the council in Athens, among people whose gods aren't yours. how do you describe the human race?
o: divided by nature into peoples who can't understand each other.
made of one, to dwell on the whole face of the earth.
best left to each city to define.
games.why: "hath made of one, all mankind." Paul starts with what he and the Athenians share before anything that divides them.

practice: Choose a place far from you, a country in the news this week, the place your clothes were sewn, a region you know almost nothing about, and let it be real people, not a map: someone waking up there, cooking, worrying about a child, laughing at something.
If you pray, pray for them, as Catholics do in the prayers of the faithful at Mass; if you don't, hold them in mind as family you haven't met.

wordCard.voice: Solidarity. One human family, made of one, where one member's pain and joy belong to all, held as a firm commitment, not a passing feeling. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: body. Paul's word for the many members that suffer and rejoice together.

carryVoice: Your line: one family. Cousins you haven't met yet, on the far side of every newscast. See you tomorrow.
